result.markdown: --- title: "Why Eigenvectors?" subtitle: "A tour of spectral methods" author: "CMSC 35410 · Lecture 1" format: revealjs: theme: [default, theme.scss] slide-number: c/t hash: true center: false transition: none width: 1100 height: 720 margin: 0.06 html-math-method: mathjax fig-format: svg fig-align: center jupyter: python3 execute: echo: false warning: false --- # §0 Course overview {background-color="#1c1b19"} ## Motivation Spectral methods are a powerful tool for understanding complex systems by studying the **eigenvalues and eigenvectors** of associated linear operators. Because their theory generalizes from **finite-dimensional** linear algebra to **infinite-dimensional settings**, they provide a unifying framework for the analysis and computation of a wide range of problems. ## Tentative Topic List: Spectral methods in finite dimensions - Spectral Graph Theory - Random Walks Over Graphs and Their Convergence - Spectral Clustering - Cheeger's Inequality - Modern Spectral Algorithms via Semidefinite Programming - Spectral Sparsification - Expander Graphs and Their Significance - Markov Chains Mixing Times and Log-Sobolev Inequalities - Method of Moments for Latent-Variable Models ## Tentative Topic List: Spectral methods in infinite dimensions - Sturm-Liouville Theory and Spectral Decomposition - Markov Processes in Continuous Space and Their Generators - Brownian Motion and the Laplacian - Langevin Dynamics and the Fokker-Planck Equation - Bakry-Emery Theory - Manifold Learning and Diffusion Maps - Spectral Collocation Methods ## Eigenvectors, Eigenvalues and Diagonalization __Definition__: An **eigenvector** of a matrix $A$ is a nonzero vector $\mathbf{v}$ such that $$ A \mathbf{v} = \lambda \mathbf{v} $$ for some scalar $\lambda$, called the **eigenvalue** corresponding to $\mathbf{v}$. __Spectral Decomposition__: A matrix $A$ is diagonalizable if it can be written as $$ A = V \Lambda V^{-1}, $$ where the columns of $V$ are the eigenvectors of $A$ and $\Lambda$ is a diagonal matrix containing the corresponding eigenvalues. __NB1__: Not all matrices are diagonalizable. In such cases, we may need to consider generalized eigenvectors and the Jordan canonical form. __NB2__: When $A$ is symmetric, it is always diagonalizable with an orthonormal set of eigenvectors. ## Why Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues Matter __Variational Interpretation__:Eigenvectors and eigenvalues are solutions of optimization problems: $$ \lambda_{\max}(A) = \max_{\mathbf{v} \neq 0} \frac{\mathbf{v}^\top A \mathbf{v}}{\mathbf{v}^\top \mathbf{v}} $$ This can be generalized to other eigenvalues and their corresponding eigenvectors (see the Courant-Fischer min-max theorem in review notes). __Geometric Interpretation__: Eigenvectors indicate directions in which the linear transformation associated with the matrix acts by __simply scaling__, and the corresponding eigenvalues indicate the scaling factor. For a symmetric matrix $A$: $$ A = Q \Lambda Q^\top = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i \mathbf{q}_i \mathbf{q}_i^\top, $$ a weighted sum of projections onto the eigenvectors. ## Why Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues Matter 2 __Variational Interpretation__:Eigenvectors and eigenvalues are solutions of optimization problems. __Geometric Interpretation__: Eigenvectors indicate directions in which the linear transformation associated with the matrix acts by __simply scaling__, and the corresponding eigenvalues indicate the scaling factor. __Algebraic Interpretation__: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues provide a way to understand the structure of a matrix through its diagonalization, revealing __invariant subspaces__ and __simplifying matrix computations__. $$ A^t \mathbf{u} = Q \lambda^t Q^{-1} \mathbf{u} $$ This is super-useful for solving linear ODEs: $$ \mathbf{\dot{x}}(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t) \to \mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At} \mathbf{x}(0) = Q e^{\Lambda t} Q^{-1} \mathbf{x}(0). $$ ## Show of hands {.center} - Who has used **PCA**? - Who has run a **clustering** algorithm? - Who has, today, typed something into a **search engine**? . . . ::: box Everyone here has already used a spectral method today, probably without the label. ::: ::: notes \~2 min. The pitch for the whole course: this is a move you already rely on. ::: ## The strategy this course is about {.smaller} > Take something that looks intractable (combinatorial, continuous, noisy) and turn it into **"compute the eigenvalues / eigenvectors of some linear operator."** . . . Today's tour visits communities that rarely read each other's papers: | | Community | Operator | |------------------------|------------------------|------------------------| | §1 | Web search | Google matrix $M$ (not symmetric) | | §2–3 | Graph partitioning | Graph Laplacian $L$, $\mathcal L$ | | §4 | Statistics / ML | Covariance matrix, SVD | | §5 | Geometry / physics | Heat semigroup $e^{-tL}$, Laplace–Beltrami $\Delta$ | | §6–7 | Numerical analysis | Differential operators, Chebyshev / Fourier bases | # §1 · The hook: PageRank {background-color="#1c1b19"} ## A random surfer Web = directed graph $G=(V,E)$. The surfer follows a random out-link, but with probability $1-\alpha$ teleports to a uniformly random page: $$ M \;=\; \alpha P + (1-\alpha)\,\tfrac1n \mathbf 1\mathbf 1^\top . $$ . . . The **PageRank** vector is a *left eigenvector with eigenvalue 1*: $$ \pi^\top M = \pi^\top . $$ . . . **Perron–Frobenius:** $M$ is strictly positive and stochastic, so $\pi$ exists, is unique, and is entrywise positive. ::: notes §1 total \~12 min. Perron–Frobenius (informal): strictly positive irreducible matrix ⇒ real, simple, largest-modulus eigenvalue with positive eigenvector. ::: ## The algorithm *is* the eigenvector computation Power iteration: $\;\pi_{k+1}^\top = \pi_k^\top M$. . . . Why it converges: teleportation is a **contraction** in $\ell_1$. A difference of probability vectors sums to $0$, so the teleport term drops out: $$ \|\pi_{k+1} - \pi\|_1 = \alpha\,\big\|(\pi_k - \pi)^\top P\big\|_1 \;\le\; \alpha\,\|\pi_k - \pi\|_1,\\ \qquad\text{so}\qquad \|\pi_k - \pi\|_1 \le 2\,\alpha^k . $$ Spectrally: $$\;\operatorname{spec}(M) = \{1\} \cup \alpha\cdot\{\lambda_2(P),\dots,\lambda_n(P)\},$$ so the **spectral gap** is $1 - |\lambda_2(M)| \ge 1 - \alpha$. . . . ::: box **Discussion:** what does a *small* spectral gap mean physically for the surfer? ::: ::: notes Answer: slow mixing — the surfer's distribution takes a long time to forget where it started. Same phenomenon as Markov chain mixing time; formalized with graph spectral gaps in a few weeks. Contraction proof: for probability vectors $x,y$, $z = x-y$ has $z^\top\mathbf 1 = 0$, so $z^\top M = \alpha z^\top P + \tfrac{1-\alpha}{n}(z^\top\mathbf 1)\mathbf 1^\top = \alpha z^\top P$; $P$ row-stochastic gives $\|z^\top P\|_1 \le \|z\|_1$. Apply with $x = \pi_k$, $y = \pi$. Eigenvalue proof (Haveliwala–Kamvar 2003): if $x^\top M = \lambda x^\top$ with $\lambda \ne 1$, then $M\mathbf 1 = \mathbf 1$ forces $x^\top\mathbf 1 = 0$, hence $x^\top P = (\lambda/\alpha)x^\top$, so $|\lambda| \le \alpha$. Equality iff $P$ has a second unimodular eigenvalue (e.g. two closed components). Assumes dangling pages are patched so $P$ is row-stochastic. Why prefer the contraction: $M$ is non-normal, so the eigenvalue bound only gives $C|\lambda_2(M)|^k$ with $C$ depending on eigenvector conditioning; the $\ell_1$ argument has constant 1 and holds for every $k$. That is the dashed $\alpha^k$ line in the demo. Well-mixed graph: $|\lambda_2(P)|$ small, so the error beats $\alpha^k$ by a lot; two communities: $\lambda_2(P) \approx 1$, error tracks $\alpha^k$. ::: ## Demo: power iteration {.smaller} open in new tab ↗ ::: notes Run on the well-mixed web first (α = 0.85), then switch to "Two communities" and push α toward 0.97. The orange faint curve is the other graph at the same α. Point out: the αᵏ line is only an upper bound — the well-mixed graph beats it by a lot, the two-community graph barely does. ::: ## A remark to flag now, pay off later $M$ comes from a **directed** graph, so it is generally - not symmetric, - not even **normal** ($MM^* \neq M^*M$), - with left and right eigenvectors that differ. No inner product makes it self-adjoint: no diagonal reweighting enforces detailed balance on a generic directed graph. ::: warn Perron–Frobenius still gives a real, positive dominant eigenvalue — but the clean orthogonal-eigenbasis picture of the spectral theorem is **not** operating here. ::: ::: notes Hold that thought — it resurfaces in §2, in reverse. ::: # §2 · From graphs to eigenvectors: spectral clustering {background-color="#1c1b19"} ## Partitioning a graph Weighted undirected graph, adjacency $A$, degrees $D$, Laplacian $$ L = D - A, \qquad x^\top L x = \sum_{(i,j)\in E} w_{ij}(x_i - x_j)^2 \;\ge 0, \qquad L\mathbf 1 = 0 . $$ . . . Goal: clusters with few crossing edges (Conductance/Normalized Cut Objective). **NP-hard** as stated. . . . Relax the $\pm1$ indicator to any real vector: $$ \min_{\mathbf{x}^\top D\mathbf 1 = 0}\; \frac{\mathbf{x}^\top L \mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{x}^\top D \mathbf{x}} \;=\; \lambda_2(L), $$ attained **exactly** by the **Fiedler vector** $v_2$. ::: notes §2 total \~15 min. The Rayleigh quotient on the board: extrema over the unit sphere are the extreme eigenvalues; Courant–Fischer gives the rest. ::: ## Demo: thresholding the Fiedler vector {.smaller} open in new tab ↗ ::: notes Start in "True layout". Then "Scrambled" — the algorithm never saw the geometry, only the edges; colors still separate the blobs. Then "Ordered by Fiedler". Increase bridge weight / count: λ₂ grows, the gap to λ₃ closes, clustering gets worse. The Cheeger readout at the bottom previews §3. ::: ## Self-adjointness, precisely For **any** undirected weighted graph (no regularity needed): - $L_{rw} = D^{-1}L$ and $P = D^{-1}A$ are self-adjoint w.r.t. $\langle x,y\rangle_D = x^\top D y$ — this is exactly **detailed balance** for $\pi \propto \deg$; - $\mathcal L = D^{1/2} L_{rw} D^{-1/2}$ is the *same operator*, self-adjoint w.r.t. the standard inner product. . . . ::: box A change of **which inner product** you measure against — not a repair of a broken operator. Undirected graphs get this for free; directed graphs (§1) generally do not. ::: ::: notes This is Exercise 4 in the Linear Algebra Review note — assign before or after this lecture. ::: # §3 · A real theorem: Cheeger's inequality {background-color="#1c1b19"} ## An eigenvalue certifies a bottleneck {.smaller} Conductance of $G$: $$ h(G) = \min_{S}\; \frac{|\partial S|}{\min\big(\mathrm{vol}(S),\, \mathrm{vol}(V\setminus S)\big)} . $$ . . . **Cheeger's inequality.** With $\lambda_2$ the second-smallest eigenvalue of $\mathcal L$, $$ \frac{\lambda_2}{2} \;\le\; h(G) \;\le\; \sqrt{2\lambda_2} . $$ . . . - Not a heuristic: a **two-sided, provable** certificate. - The upper bound is constructive: a **sweep cut** of $D^{-1/2}v_2$ achieves it (the dashed line in the demo). - Proof later in the term; then SDP relaxations (ARV) and sparsification (Spielman–Teng). ::: notes \~10 min. Goal today is the shape of the result, not the proof. Fill in the week number for the proof. ::: # §4 · The bridge everyone already knows: PCA / SVD {background-color="#1c1b19"} ## The spectral theorem PCA computes eigenvectors of the (symmetric, PSD) covariance matrix. Time to state what §2–3 were quietly leaning on: ::: box **Spectral theorem.** If $A = A^*$ on an $n$-dimensional inner product space, there is an orthonormal basis $v_1,\dots,v_n$ of eigenvectors with **real** eigenvalues: $$A = Q\Lambda Q^*, \qquad Q \text{ unitary}.$$ ::: . . . **SVD** is the rectangular generalization: $A = U\Sigma V^*$. **Eckart–Young.** $A_k = \sum_{i\le k} \sigma_i u_i v_i^*$ is the best rank-$k$ approximation in Frobenius and operator norm: $\;\|A - A_k\|_F^2 = \sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2 .$ ::: notes §4 total \~12 min. This is the result every student has used via sklearn without knowing it's a spectral-theorem statement dressed up. ::: ## Demo: PCA on synthetic data ::: {#8a69a51c .cell fig-height='4.6' fig-width='11' execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lecture1_files/figure-revealjs/cell-2-output-1.png){} ::: ::: ::: notes Blue dots sit exactly on the orange line: the reconstruction error is predicted by the discarded singular values, and nothing of rank k does better (grey = random subspace). ::: ## The framing line > "Every example so far that behaved nicely — orthogonal eigenvectors, real eigenvalues, stable numerics — was secretly symmetric, or could be made symmetric. PageRank's matrix was not, and we saw the clean picture partially break. **Much of this course is about knowing which case you're in before you start computing.**" # §5 · Diffusion and the shape of things {background-color="#1c1b19"} ## Heat on a graph $$ \frac{du}{dt} = -Lu,\quad u(0)=u_0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad u(t) = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}\,\langle u_0, v_k\rangle\, v_k . $$ . . . - $\lambda_1 = 0$: the constant mode survives forever (equilibrium). - Every other mode decays at its own rate $e^{-\lambda_k t}$. - The **slowest** non-constant mode is $v_2$ — the Fiedler vector again. . . . ::: box Same eigenvector, two jobs: "the best 2-way cut" **and** "the last non-uniform heat left before equilibrium." ::: ::: notes §5 total \~12–15 min. Loosely follows the opening of Rosenberg, *The Laplacian on a Riemannian Manifold*. Qualitative today. ::: ## Demo: watching heat diffuse {.smaller} open in new tab ↗ ::: notes Cycle first: press Play; the blue curve is the continuous heat kernel on a circle of the same length (Fourier eigenbasis) — discrete and continuous agree once the high modes are gone. Then "Two clusters + bridge": after the high modes die, what remains is exactly the orange Fiedler mode — one cluster warm, the other cool. Path: slowest of all (λ₂ ≈ π²/n²). ::: ## From graphs to manifolds Replace the graph by a compact Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ and $L$ by the **Laplace–Beltrami operator** $\Delta = -\operatorname{div}\operatorname{grad}$: - self-adjoint, $\Delta \succeq 0$, discrete spectrum $0 = \lambda_1 < \lambda_2 \le \cdots \to \infty$; - eigenfunctions $\phi_k$ form an orthonormal basis of $L^2(M)$. . . . Heat equation $\partial_t u = -\Delta u$, solved by the heat kernel $$ K(t,x,y) = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}\,\phi_k(x)\,\phi_k(y). $$ The **same equation** as the graph case — a finite sum becomes a discrete-but-infinite one. ::: notes The eigenbasis comes from Theorem 4.1 in the Linear Algebra Review note, applied to the compact self-adjoint resolvent (I+Δ)⁻¹. ::: ## Where the geometry hides {.smaller} Heat trace, as $t \to 0^+$ (Minakshisundaram–Pleijel): $$ Z(t) = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t} \;\sim\; (4\pi t)^{-n/2}\Big(\mathrm{Vol}(M) + \tfrac{t}{6}\!\int_M \mathrm{Scal}\,dV + O(t^2)\Big). $$ From the list of eigenvalues alone you read off: - the **dimension** $n$ (rate of blow-up), - the **volume** (leading coefficient), - the **total scalar curvature** (next coefficient). . . . **Weyl's law**, from the other end: $$N(\lambda) = \#\{k: \lambda_k \le \lambda\} \;\sim\; \frac{\omega_n \mathrm{Vol}(M)}{(2\pi)^n}\,\lambda^{n/2}.$$ ## Can one hear the shape of a drum? :::::: columns ::: {.column width="55%"} **Kac (1966):** a drum's shape determines its frequencies. Can you run that backward? . . . **Gordon–Webb–Wolpert (1992): no.** Two non-isometric planar drums with identical spectra. ::: :::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.box .small} The spectrum determines a great deal (dimension, volume, curvature, bottlenecks, …) — but **not everything**. Where exactly the line falls is a theme we return to. ::: :::: :::::: . . . Either way, actually **computing** with a continuous operator like $\Delta$ is a real numerical problem. → ::: notes "Spectral" for eigenvalue problems comes from the analogy with spectral lines in physics. ::: # §6 · Spectral methods for differential equations {background-color="#1c1b19"} ## Same word, different community Solve $\;u'' = e^{4x}$ on $[-1,1]$, $\;u(\pm1)=0$. - **Finite differences:** local stencils, error $O(N^{-2})$. - **Chebyshev collocation:** global polynomial basis, error $O(\rho^{-N})$ for smooth $u$ — "spectral" convergence. ::: {#455a2277 .cell fig-height='3.9' fig-width='10' execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lecture1_files/figure-revealjs/cell-3-output-1.png){} ::: ::: ::: notes §6 \~15 min. The intended "wow": \~20 Chebyshev points reach machine precision; finite differences with thousands of points are still around 1e-6. Mention Orr–Sommerfeld (next slide) as a name-drop. ::: ## Planting a seed: non-normal operators The **Orr–Sommerfeld** operator (hydrodynamic stability) is **not self-adjoint**. - Eigenvalues alone can badly mislead about its behavior. - Transient growth, sensitivity to perturbation → **pseudospectra**. ::: warn Same warning as PageRank, now for differential operators. We return to this once we have the machinery. ::: # §7 · Payoff: spectral methods run the weather {background-color="#1c1b19"} ## Spherical harmonics and the global forecast Operational global forecasting has long used the **spectral transform method**: expand fields in spherical harmonics (eigenfunctions of $\Delta$ on $S^2$). - Smooth global fields ⇒ exponential convergence (as in §6). - A modest number of degrees of freedom buys enormous accuracy. ::: box Not a classroom curiosity: part of why a global forecast is computationally tractable at all. ::: ::: notes \~5 min. Currency check before lecture: confirm current operational models' numerics before citing specifics (e.g. ECMWF IFS), since this has been an active area of change. ::: ## Roadmap for the semester - **Spectral graph theory proper:** expanders, mixing times, Cheeger's inequality (proved). - **Spectral algorithms in ML:** clustering, embeddings, low-rank models, diffusion maps. - **The recurring question underneath all of it:** ::: box What do we actually need — **self-adjointness, normality, or just diagonalizability** — and what breaks when we don't have it? ::: PageRank and directed graphs were today's first data point. More will come. # Appendix: definitions for the board {background-color="#1c1b19"} ## Operators and the spectral theorem {.defs} **Inner product / adjoint.** On $\mathbb F^n$, $\langle x,y\rangle = y^*x$. The adjoint satisfies $\langle Ax,y\rangle = \langle x,A^*y\rangle$. $A$ is **self-adjoint** if $A=A^*$; **normal** if $AA^* = A^*A$ (orthonormal eigenbasis, possibly complex eigenvalues). **Spectral theorem.** $A=A^*$ on an $n$-dim inner product space ⇒ orthonormal eigenbasis, real eigenvalues $\lambda_1\ge\dots\ge\lambda_n$; $A = Q\Lambda Q^*$. **Rayleigh quotient.** $R_A(x) = \langle Ax,x\rangle / \langle x,x\rangle$; extrema on the unit sphere are the extreme eigenvalues (Courant–Fischer gives the rest). **Perron–Frobenius (informal).** Strictly positive irreducible matrix ⇒ real, simple, largest-in-modulus eigenvalue with a strictly positive eigenvector. **SVD / Eckart–Young.** $A = U\Sigma V^*$; $A_k = \sum_{i\le k}\sigma_i u_i v_i^*$ is the best rank-$k$ approximation in Frobenius and operator norm. ## Graphs {.defs} For $G=(V,E,w)$ undirected, symmetric adjacency $A$, $D = \mathrm{diag}(\deg)$: - $L = D - A$: symmetric, PSD, $\mathbf 1\in\ker L$. - $L_{rw} = D^{-1}L$, $\;P = D^{-1}A$. - $\mathcal L = D^{-1/2}LD^{-1/2} = I - D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}$. **Degree-weighted inner product** $\langle x,y\rangle_D = x^\top D y$: $L_{rw}$ and $P$ are self-adjoint w.r.t. it; $\mathcal L = D^{1/2}L_{rw}D^{-1/2}$ is self-adjoint w.r.t. the standard one. **Conductance** $h(G) = \min_S |\partial S| / \min(\mathrm{vol}(S),\mathrm{vol}(V\setminus S))$. **Cheeger:** $\lambda_2(\mathcal L)/2 \le h(G) \le \sqrt{2\lambda_2(\mathcal L)}$. **Heat semigroup.** $u(t) = e^{-tL}u_0 = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}\langle u_0,v_k\rangle v_k$; kernel $K_t = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}v_kv_k^\top$. ## Manifolds and numerics {.defs} **Laplace–Beltrami.** On compact $(M,g)$, $\Delta = -\operatorname{div}\operatorname{grad}$ is self-adjoint, $\Delta\succeq0$, spectrum $0=\lambda_1<\lambda_2\le\cdots\to\infty$, eigenfunctions $\phi_k$ an ONB of $L^2(M)$. Heat kernel $K(t,x,y) = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}\phi_k(x)\phi_k(y)$. **Heat trace.** $Z(t) = \operatorname{Tr} e^{-t\Delta} \sim (4\pi t)^{-n/2}\big(\mathrm{Vol}(M) + \tfrac t6\int_M \mathrm{Scal}\,dV + O(t^2)\big)$. **Weyl's law.** $N(\lambda) \sim \dfrac{\omega_n\mathrm{Vol}(M)}{(2\pi)^n}\lambda^{n/2}$. **Spectral convergence.** For smooth data, global (Chebyshev/Fourier) bases converge faster than any power of $1/N$; local finite-difference stencils converge at a fixed polynomial rate.
